Chapter 3: The Joy and Wonder at the Heart of Faith
You ever notice how there’s a kind of happiness that just can’t be explained by how well things are going, or how comfortable life feels? It’s the kind of joy you get when you catch a child’s laughter, or spot those very first flowers pushing through after a long winter. It’s not about getting what you want—it’s about being surprised by beauty, showing up right where you never expected.
But let’s be honest, most of us lose track of that feeling as we get older. Daily routines, work, all those responsibilities... they have a way of making the world look a little gray, a little too predictable. Still, every now and then, something breaks through. Maybe it’s a burst of laughter, a sudden flash of insight, or just noticing something extraordinary tucked inside the ordinary.
I want you to picture this: one evening, after a long, exhausting day, a parent is just sitting quietly in their living room, watching the kids play. The place is messy, bills are stacked up, and the future feels more than a little uncertain. Yet somehow, in that moment, all those worries melt away. The sound of the kids laughing, the warmth in the room—it suddenly feels like a gift. Not something earned, or deserved, but something wonderful that just arrived.
That’s when it hits you: joy isn’t something you can force or control. It sneaks up on you, a gentle reminder that the world is a whole lot bigger—and more mysterious—than you ever thought. The old faith, with all its wild stories and mysteries, always made space for this kind of joy. It taught that life isn’t just a list of facts to memorize—it’s a place full of wonder.
Now, here’s something to pay attention to. A lot of modern philosophies, searching for certainty, have drained life of its color. Miracles get explained away, mysteries are dismissed, and everything’s reduced to what can be measured or weighed. But the truth is, that misses the point. The world isn’t some problem to solve—it’s a gift we’re meant to receive.
Think of a friend who spent years chasing success. Eventually, they realized the things that really matter can’t be bought or earned. Laughter with friends, the beauty of a sunset, the comfort of a familiar song—these are the moments that actually give life meaning.
And you start to see, faith isn’t just about following rules or memorizing doctrines. It’s about getting back that sense of childlike wonder. The old faith invited us to see the world as an adventure, packed with surprises and possibilities. It didn’t run from mystery—it welcomed it, seeing it as a sign of something even greater.
Most of us don’t realize just how much we need that sense of wonder until it’s gone. Without it, life turns into a checklist of tasks, instead of a story worth living. The old faith, with all its paradoxes and big mysteries, offered a way of seeing that made room for both reason and imagination.
